title: The Guru's alphabet
hook: Gurmukhi, from the Guru's mouth, has thirty-five letters and a set of vowel signs

segments.voice: Yesterday, camp three closed, and you wrote seven small lines. Your line was you can do this. Did the first line of your rhythm happen this morning? Day one hundred fifty-seven.

Plastic letters on a fridge door. A for apple, B for ball. Before a child can read a single word, they can make the sounds, and they'll say them to anyone who'll listen. Today a new camp begins, and it begins the same way, with letters. For the next seventy-five days we'll read one text together, slowly: Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib, the first hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib. To do that, it helps to meet the script it's written in.
screen: `MAGNETS ON THE FRIDGE.` → `A NEW CAMP: THE TEXT.` → `JAPJI SAHIB, LINE BY LINE.`

segments.voice: The script is Gurmukhi. Gur is Guru. Mukhi comes from mukh, the mouth. From the mouth of the Guru. Sikhs trace it to Guru Angad, the second Guru, who, tradition says, shaped and settled the letters so the Sikhs could write down Guru Nanak's hymns. The letters grew out of older scripts already used in Punjab; Guru Angad gave them a form, and a purpose. The alphabet is called the painti, which simply means thirty-five, because it has thirty-five basic letters. It opens with three letters that carry vowels, oora, aira and eeree, and then the consonants march in neat rows: sassa, haha, then kakka, khakha, gagga, and on. Around the letters sit a set of vowel signs, small marks above, below and beside them, that change the sound. Later, a handful of extra letters with a dot at the foot were added for sounds borrowed from Persian, so modern charts show a few more than thirty-five. Here's the gift for a learner: Gurmukhi is close to phonetic. Mostly, you say what you see. So you can sound out Japji long before you understand it, the way a child sings a song before knowing what the words mean. And, as you saw on day four, the very first character of the Guru Granth Sahib isn't a letter at all. It's the numeral one, joined to the letter oora, with a long curve sweeping over the top: Ik Onkar. The One, who is everywhere. The whole scripture begins with a number and a sound. So in this camp, we read with the mouth first. Understanding follows.
screen: `GURMUKHI — FROM THE GURU'S MOUTH.` · `GURU ANGAD SETTLES THE LETTERS.` · `THE PAINTI — THIRTY-FIVE.` · `SAY WHAT YOU SEE.` · then, large: `IK ONKAR.`

segments.voice: Look at the symbol on the screen: Ik Onkar. Lift one finger, and trace it in the air, slowly, as if you're writing on a window. First the numeral one. Then the round letter beside it. Then the long curve that sweeps up over the top and keeps going. Do it three times, a little smoother each time. Then rest your hand in your lap, breathe, and let the shape stay behind your eyes. If you pray, you can say Ik Onkar quietly as you trace. The bell holds the time.
Gurmukhi. From the Guru's mouth: the script of the Guru Granth Sahib, with thirty-five letters and a set of vowel signs.
Your line: read with the mouth first. Today, find Gurmukhi somewhere, a sign, a food label, a screen, and try saying one letter out loud. Day one hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikh children often learn the Gurmukhi letters at gurdwara Punjabi classes, reciting the painti aloud, so that they can read Gurbani for themselves.
